title: How do you model a composite primary key in JPA, and what is the difference between @EmbeddedId and @IdClass?
keyPoints: @EmbeddedId uses one @Embeddable key class as a single field on the entity; access parts via id.getAccountId().
@IdClass keeps separate @Id fields on the entity plus a mirror key class whose field names and types match the entity's @Id fields.
Both require the key class to be Serializable, have a no-arg constructor, and implement equals and hashCode over all key fields.
JPQL with @EmbeddedId navigates through the key: WHERE s.id.accountId = :acc.
JPQL with @IdClass reads naturally: WHERE s.accountId = :acc because the fields sit directly on the entity.
@EmbeddedId is preferred because grouping the key into one object models the identity as a real concept and reduces mistakes.

s1_definition.oneliner: @EmbeddedId embeds one @Embeddable key object (access via getId().getX()); @IdClass keeps separate @Id fields on the entity plus a mirror key class, and both need Serializable, equals, and hashCode.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Composite primary key** – a key made of two or more columns together, where neither column alone is unique but the combination is.
- **@EmbeddedId** – uses a single @Embeddable key class annotated on one field of the entity; you access the parts through the key object, e.g., statement.getId().getAccountId().
- **@IdClass** – keeps the key fields as separate @Id fields directly on the entity, plus a plain non-entity mirror class listed in @IdClass(...) whose field names and types match.
- **Key class requirements** – both approaches require the key class to be Serializable, to have a public no-arg constructor, and to implement equals and hashCode over all key fields.
- **@MapsId** – when a composite key column is also a foreign key (derived identity), @MapsId lets a @ManyToOne share a key column with the composite key.
s1_definition.analogy: A monthly account statement at National Bank of India is uniquely identified by the account number PLUS the statement period together. With @EmbeddedId you put those two values inside one little key envelope object and the statement carries that envelope. With @IdClass you keep the account number and period as two loose fields on the statement and separately describe a matching key form so the bank's filing system has one handle for the pair.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  @EmbeddedId vs @IdClass
  ============================================

  @EmbeddedId:
  +-------------------+       +--------------------+
  | MonthlyStatement  |       | StatementId        |
  |-------------------|       | (@Embeddable)      |
  | @EmbeddedId       |------>| accountId: String  |
  |   StatementId id  |       | period: String     |
  | closingBalance    |       | equals/hashCode    |
  +-------------------+       +--------------------+
  JPQL: WHERE s.id.accountId = :acc

  @IdClass:
  +-------------------+       +--------------------+
  | MonthlyStatement  |       | StatementKey       |
  |-------------------|       | (plain class)      |
  | @Id accountId     |<----->| accountId: String  |
  | @Id period        |<----->| period: String     |
  | closingBalance    |       | equals/hashCode    |
  +-------------------+       +--------------------+
  @IdClass(StatementKey.class)
  JPQL: WHERE s.accountId = :acc  (more natural)

  Both require:
  - Serializable
  - No-arg constructor
  - equals + hashCode on ALL key fields
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A composite primary key is an identity made of two or more columns that are unique only in combination, and JPA gives two ways to map it. With @EmbeddedId, Rajesh creates one key class annotated @Embeddable and the entity holds a single field of that type annotated @EmbeddedId, so the key is a first-class object that can be passed around and used in findById. With @IdClass, the key fields sit as separate @Id fields directly on the entity, and a separate mirror class in @IdClass provides the single-object identity that the persistence context needs.

Both styles require the key class to be Serializable, to have a no-arg constructor, and to implement equals and hashCode over all key fields. Hibernate uses these methods in its identity map, so a broken equals silently breaks caching and merging. In the statement service at National Bank of India, the monthly statement is identified by the account id and the period together, modelled with @EmbeddedId so the key is one immutable value object.

Pankaj defaults to @EmbeddedId because grouping the key into one object models the identity as a real concept and reduces mistakes, and reaches for @IdClass only when the id fields should sit directly on the entity for simpler JPQL or to match a legacy schema. He builds composite keys from stable, immutable business values like an account id and a period that never change.

Remember one sentence: @EmbeddedId groups the composite key into one embeddable object, @IdClass keeps separate @Id fields with a mirror class, and both require Serializable with correct equals and hashCode.
